main.text: [III, 56] Chapter XXVI. [col. 303]
It is proved from the Arabic language that רחם racham is a species of vulture.

Now, given the hesitation of the interpreters that we have described, who would deny that it is safest to consult the Arabs? For the bird رخم [rakham] racham, or رخمة [rakhama] rachama, is very well known among them even today, and it is described by many, as what follows will make plain. Damir: الرخمة طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة [al-rakhama ṭāyir abqaʿ yushbih al-nasr fī al-khilqa] Rachama, a bird of variegated colour, approaching the nature of the eagle. And a little later: وفي طبع هذا الطاير انه لا يرضي من الجبال الا من بالوحش منها ولا من الاماكن الا بالاسحقها والابعدها من اماكن اعداية ولا من الهضاب الا بصخورها ويقال لها لانوق [wa-fī ṭabʿ hādhā al-ṭāyir annahu lā yarḍī min al-jibāl illā min bi-l-waḥsh minhā wa-lā min al-amākin illā bi-l-asḥaqihā wa-l-abʿadihā min amākin aʿdāyih wa-lā min al-hiḍāb illā bi-ṣukhūrihā wa-yuqāl lahā lānūq] It is the nature of this bird that it does not like mountains unless they are extremely solitary; nor other places, unless they are very far apart and most remote from inhabited places; and among rocky places only inaccessible crags. It is called by another name anuk. And below: وتبيض بيضة واحدة وربما اتامت وهي من ليام الطير وهن ثلاث الغراب والبوم والرخم والعرب تضرب المثل في الامتناع ببيضها فيقولون اعز من بيض الانوق وابعد من بيض الانوق فانه لا يكاد [col. 304] يظفر به لان اوكارها في روس الجبال والاماكن الصعبة كما تقدم قال الشاعر ۞ [wa-tabīḍ bayḍa wāḥida wa-rubbamā atāmat wa-hiya min liyām al-ṭayr wa-hunna thalāth al-ghurāb wa-l-būm wa-l-rakham wa-l-ʿarab taḍrib al-mathal fī al-imtināʿ bi-bayḍihā fa-yaqūlūn aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq wa-abʿad min bayḍ al-anūq fa-innahu lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī rūs al-jibāl wa-l-amākin al-ṣaʿba kamā taqaddam qāla al-shāʿir]
وكنت اذا استودعت سر ۞ اكتمت كبيض انوق لا ينال لها وكر ۞ [wa-kuntu idhā istawdaʿtu sirr aktamtu ka-bayḍ anūq lā yunāl lahā wakr]

And it lays a single egg, but sometimes it also produces twins. It is one of the birds called liam (as if you were to say ignoble). These are three: the raven, the little owl and the racham. There is a proverb among the Arabs signifying how inaccessible its eggs are: “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”, or “More remote than the egg of the anuk”: for hardly anyone reaches it, because it nests on the summit of mountains and in precipitous places, as was said before. Hence the poet said: “And when I was called apart into a hidden place, I was concealed like the egg of the anuk, whose nest is inaccessible”. Alkazuinius: رخمه طاير النسر في خلقته يختار لبيضه اطراف الجبال [III, 57] الشاهقة ليصعب الوصول الي بيضه يقال اعز من بيض الانوق فاذا جاء اوان بيضها ذهبت الي الهند واتت حجر يقال له ابوطاقيون وهو حجر مدور مثل خرزة اذا حركت تعقعق في جوفه حجر اخر ويترك ذلك الحجر تحتها فتبيض من غير وجع وتطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من جيف [rakhama ṭāyir al-nasr fī khilqatih yakhtār li-bayḍih aṭrāf al-jibāl al-shāhiqa li-yaṣʿub al-wuṣūl ilā bayḍih yuqāl aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq fa-idhā jāʾa awān bayḍihā dhahabat ilā al-hind wa-atat ḥajar yuqāl lahu abūṭāqiyūn wa-huwa ḥajar mudawwar mithl kharaza idhā ḥurrikat taʿaqʿaqa fī jawfih ḥajar ākhar wa-yutrak dhālika al-ḥajar taḥtahā fa-tabīḍ min ghayr wajaʿ wa-taṭīr khalf al-ʿasākir li-taʾkul min jiyaf] Rachama is an eagle bird (that is, of the aquiline kind). It is its nature to choose the summits of the highest mountains for its eggs, so that access to them may be more difficult. Hence the saying, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk” (that is, of the rachama). When it is about to lay its eggs, it goes to India and brings from there a stone which they call abutacium (rather, εὐτόκιον [eutokion]). This stone is round like a pearl. When it is moved, another stone sounds inside it. With this stone placed under itself, it lays its eggs without pain. It follows armies in its flight, to feed on the corpses of the slain. Alcamus: الانوق العقاب الرخمة وطاير اسود له كالعرف او اسود اصلع الراس اصفر المنقار وهو اعز من بيض الانوق لانها تحرزها فلا يكاد يظفر به لان اوكارها في التلل الصعبة قيل [col. 305] فاخلاقها عشر خصال تحصن بيضها وتحمي فرجها وتالف ولدها ولا تمكن من نفسها غير زوجها وتقطع في اول القواطع وترجع في اول الرواجع وتطير في التحسير ولا تغتر بالشكير ولا ترب بالوكور ولا تسقط علي الجفر بالشكير [al-anūq al-ʿuqāb al-rakhama wa-ṭāyir aswad lahu ka-l-ʿurf aw aswad aṣlaʿ al-raʾs aṣfar al-minqār wa-huwa aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq li-annahā taḥruzuhā fa-lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī al-tilal al-ṣaʿba qīla fa-akhlāquhā ʿashar khiṣāl tuḥaṣṣin bayḍahā wa-taḥmī farkhahā wa-taʾlaf waladahā wa-lā tumakkin min nafsihā ghayr zawjihā wa-taqṭaʿ fī awwal al-qawāṭiʿ wa-tarjiʿ fī awwal al-rawājiʿ wa-taṭīr fī al-taḥsīr wa-lā taghtarr bi-l-shakīr wa-lā tarubb bi-l-wukūr wa-lā tasquṭ ʿalā al-jafr bi-l-shakīr] Anuk, a kind of eagle, which is also called rachama. A black bird, which has something like a mane. Others say: a black bird with a bald head and a yellow beak, about which there is the proverb, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”; because it guards its egg so well that it can hardly be attacked. For it nests in inaccessible mountains. Ten peculiarities are attributed to it. 1. It protects its eggs. 2. It guards its young. 3. It always stays close to its offspring. 4. It does nothing on its own without its mate. 5. It migrates with the first migrants. 6. It returns with the first to return. 7. It flies during the moulting of its feathers. 8. Nor is it endangered by the scantiness of its feathers. 9. Nor does it remain in the nest. 10. Nor does it fall into an inability to mate: as the other birds do when their feathers have fallen out. Of these ten peculiarities the first four are also found in Damir, in almost the same words. Andreas Bellunensis: Alrachame is a large bird like a kite, with white body plumage and black wing feathers. It eats putrid flesh and the like. In [III, 58] Syria it is abundant ^{(1)}. On the Sura of the Qur'an الاخراب [al-akhrāb] Alachrab, which in the Latin translator is Azoara 43, where Moses is treated, towards the end, the Commentator Abulabas Cordubensis says: لم يعرف موضع قبره الا الرخم فلذلك جعله الله اصم ابكم [lam yaʿrif mawḍiʿ qabrih illā al-rakham fa-li-dhālika jaʿalahu allāh aṣamm abkam] No one knew the place of his tomb except the bird racham, and therefore God made it deaf and dumb. This is entirely fabulous, like most things of such triflers. For, to say nothing of the rest, this bird is extremely vocal, like the whole aquiline and vulturine kind. Accordingly, as the Arabs often attribute any words they like to birds, as we do to bells, Zamachsari writes that the cry of the rachama sounds roughly like these words: سبحان ربي الاعلي [subḥān rabbī al-aʿlī] Sobchan rabbi alali, that is, Praise to my Lord most high.

Now if I wished to add everything that Alkazuinius, Ibnolbatrik, Avicenna, Serapion, Sariph, Abenbitar, Alcamus and other Arabs say about the medicinal virtues of this bird, the matter would grow beyond measure. It will therefore suffice for us to add a few things out of many, from which it may be clear what bird the Arabs call by this name. 1. The dung of the rachama expels the embryo. Alkazuinius: ذرقها ان احتملته المراة القت جنينها [dharquhā in iḥtamalathu al-marʾa alqat janīnahā], If a woman applies its dung, she expels the embryo. Avicenna: قيل ان زبله يسقط الجنين تبخيرا [qīla inna zibluhu yusqiṭu al-janīn tabkhīran], Its dung is said to expel the embryo by fumigation. Behold, the same is found in Dioscorides concerning the dung of the vulture, in the chapter On dung in book 2: Γυπὸς ἄφοδος ὑποθυμιαθεῖσα ἔμβρυα ἐκτινάσσειν παραδέδοται [gypos aphodos hypothymiatheisa embrya ektinassein paradedotai], Vulture's dung, used as a fumigation, is said to drive out the foetus. And in Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 34:
Moreover, they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, [col. 306] so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close.

2. The feather of the rachama also assists childbirth. Sariph: وان اخذت ريشه من جناحها اليمن ووضعت بين رجلي المطلغة سهل اولادها [wa-in ukhidhat rīsha min janāḥihā al-yumn wa-wuḍiʿat bayna rijlay al-muṭlagha sahhala awlādahā], When a feather is taken from its right wing and placed at the feet of a woman in labour, it relieves the pains of childbirth. So also Alcamus under رخم [rakham] racham. Pliny says the same of the vulture's feather, book 29, chapter 4: A vulture's feather placed under the feet assists women in labour. And Sextus, book 2, chapter 2: It makes them give birth without labour. [III, 59] 3. The gall of the rachama cures albugo [white opacity of the eye]. Alkazuinius: يكتحل بمرارتها وحدها لبياض العين [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā waḥdahā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn], From the vulture's gall alone an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eye. Avicenna: يكتحل بمرارتها لبياض العين بالما البارد [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn bi-l-mā al-bārid], From its gall with cold water an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eyes. The vulture's gall has the same power. Pliny, book 29, chapter 6, after saying that eagle's gall is applied as an ointment for clouding, dimness and cataracts of the eyes: The same power is also in vulture's gall, etc. Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 14:

If sluggish old age draws darkness over the eyes, drops pressed from fennel with flowing honey have been able to wipe away the ill, or the gall of the black vulture, if blades of celandine are mixed with it.

Marcellus: Combine a scruple of the gall of a cock, or of a vulture, which is far more beneficial, with an ounce of the best honey, well ground, keep it in a copper box, and use it for anointing when needed. Nothing relieves dimness more powerfully than this. Galen, Euporista, book 1, chapter 44: Vulture's gall, with juice of horehound and Attic honey, cures every dimness of the eyes and incipient cataract. Sextus: Vulture's gall, etc. dispels all dimness.

4. The liver of the rachama is useful for those possessed by a demon. Alcamus: كبده يشوي ويسحق ويسقي المجنون ثلثة ايام كل يوم ثلاث مرات ويبريه [kabiduhu yushwā wa-yusḥaqu wa-yusqā al-majnūn thalatha ayyām kull yawm thalāth marrāt wa-yubrīhi], Its liver, roasted and ground, is given to the demoniac to drink for three days, three times daily, and he recovers. So also Damir. And not much differently Abenbitar: كبدها شوي ويسحق ويداف بخل ويسقي من به جنون كل يوم ثلاث مرات ثلاثة ايام متواليه فيبريه [kabiduhā shuwiya wa-yusḥaqu wa-yudāfu bi-khall wa-yusqā man bihi junūn kull yawm thalāth marrāt thalātha ayyām mutawāliya fa-yubrīhi], Its liver is roasted, ground, and steeped in vinegar, and given to drink to one who is possessed by a demon, three times daily for three days, for three continuous days, and it heals him. Indeed, concerning epilepsy, in which there seems to be θεῖόν τι [theion ti], something divine, the older writers had handed down something similar. Pliny: Vulture's liver, drunk with its own blood for thrice seven days, is commended against epilepsy. So also Sextus and Aesculapius.

5. Here is another remedy from the flesh of the rachama! Sariph: لحم الرخم اذا خلط بخردل وجفف وبخر به المعقود عن النسا سبع [col. 307] مرات اطلقه ذلك [laḥm al-rakham idhā khuliṭa bi-khardal wa-juffifa wa-bukhkhira bihi al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā sabʿ marrāt aṭlaqahu dhālika], If the flesh of the rachama, mixed with mustard and dried, is used to fumigate a sufferer from sciatica [III, 60] seven times, he will be freed from his illness. Alcamus: التبخير بتجفيف لحمه مخلوطا بخردل سبع مرات يحل المعقود عن النسا [al-tabkhīr bi-tajfīf laḥmihi makhlūṭan bi-khardal sabʿ marrāt yaḥullu al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā], A fumigation from its dried flesh, mixed with mustard, repeated seven times, will heal one suffering from sciatica. But in both places, instead of خردل [khardal] chardal, that is, mustard, we think one should read حرمل [ḥarmal] charmal, that is, rue: because in Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 55, we find:
But if a hidden pain burns the sluggish sinews, apply the excised fat of a vulture, and rue, etc.

Moreover, for migraine and headaches remedies are prescribed by Avicenna from the rachama, and by Pliny, Galen, Marcellus, Sextus and others from the vulture. And just as the dung of the rachama in Abenbitar, Damir and Alcamus, so vulture's blood in Pliny cures leprosy. The same author, book 29, chapter 4: Among birds, the first aid against serpents is the vulture. All the Arabs with one voice attribute this power to the rachama. They report, namely, that all venomous creatures are driven off by fumigation with its feather and dung; that the bite of the viper and of scorpions is healed by smearing on its gall; and that the yellow skin which encloses the crop, dried, ground and taken in a drink, purges from every poison. On these matters, besides Avicenna, one should consult Ibnolbatrik, Abenbitar, Damir, Alcamus, etc. For there is no time to copy out their passages.

Further, they report that the rachama, or anuk, which is the same, builds its nest in inaccessible places, and that from this arose the proverb, very widely accepted among them, Rarer than the egg of the anuk. No one will deny that this fits the vulture above all. Of it the Philosopher says in the History, book 6, chapter 5: Ὁ δὲ γὺψ νεοττεύει μὲν ἐπὶ πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις· διὸ σπάνιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττούς. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρόδοτος [Ho de gyps neotteuei men epi petrais aprosbatois; dio spanion idein neotteian gypos, kai neottous. Kai dia touto Hērodotos] (read Ἡρόδωρος [Hērodōros]), ὁ Βρύσσωνος τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς γῦπας ἐφ᾽ ἑτέρας γῆς ἀδήλους [ho Bryssōnos tou Sophistou patēr, phēsin einai tous gypas eph᾽ heteras gēs adēlous] (read ἀδήλου [adēlou]) ἡμῖν τοῦτό γε λέγων τὸ σημεῖον, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε γυπὸς νεοττείαν, καὶ ὅτι πολλοὶ ἐξαίφνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι. τὸ δέ ἐστι χαλεπὸν ἰδεῖν ὦπται δ᾽ ὅμως [hēmin touto ge legōn to sēmeion, hoti oudeis heōrake gypos neotteian, kai hoti polloi exaiphnēs phainontai akolouthountes tois strateumasi. to de esti chalepon idein ōptai d᾽ homōs]. The vulture nests on inaccessible rocks; hence the vulture's nest and young are rarely seen. And therefore Herodorus, father of Bryson the Sophist, reports that vultures are from another land unknown to us, adding that this is established by the argument that, although no one has seen a vulture's nest, many suddenly appear following armies. But however difficult it is to see, it has nevertheless been seen at times. And again, book 9, chapter 11: Γυπὸς δὲ λέγεται ὑπό τινων ὡς οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν οὔτε νεοττὸν, οὔτε νεοττίαν. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρόδωρος ὁ τοῦ Βρύσωνος, τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, ἀπό τινος αὐτὸν ἑτέρας εἶναι μετεώρου γῆς ἔλεγεν, τεκμήριον τοῦτο λέγων, καὶ τὸ φαίνεσθαι ταχὺ πολλούς· ὅθεν δὲ μηδενὶ εἶναι δῆλον. τούτου δὲ αἴτιον, ὅτι τίκτει ἐν πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις [Gypos de legetai hypo tinōn hōs oudeis heōraken oute neotton, oute neottian. Alla dia touto Hērodōros ho tou Brysōnos, tou Sophistou patēr, apo tinos auton heteras einai meteōrou gēs elegen, tekmērion touto legōn, kai to phainesthai tachy pollous; hothen de mēdeni einai dēlon. toutou de aition, hoti tiktei en petrais aprosbatois].

[III, 61] Some assert that no one has seen either the young or the nest of a vulture. Therefore Herodorus, father of Bryson the Sophist, proved that they come from some higher land by this argument, that many suddenly appear, while no one knows whence they have come. But the cause of this is that the vulture breeds on inaccessible rocks. This can also be found in Antigonus, History 48. Pliny, book 10, chapter 6: No one has reached their (the vultures') nests. Hence there were even those who thought that they fly here from the opposite side of the world: falsely. For they nest on the loftiest rocks. [col. 308] Their young, indeed, are often seen. These statements do not hang together well. For if no one has reached the nest of vultures, it cannot be true that their young are often seen, since the young are not seen anywhere but in the nest or around it. But the first is taken from Herodorus, the second from Aristotle, who hold opposite views. Yet not even Aristotle said that the vulture's young are often seen, but only that they are rarely seen. Διὸ [Dio], he says, σπάνιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττοὺς [spanion idein neotteian gypos, kai neottous]; as Plutarch in the Romulus: Νεοσσοῖς γυπὸς οὐ ῥᾳδίως ἴσμεν ἐντετυχηκότες [Neossois gypos ou rhadiōs ismen entetychēkotes], We do not easily come upon the young of a vulture; in place of which the same author says in the Roman Questions: Οὐδὲ γὰρ νεοττίᾳ γυπὸς ἐντυχεῖν ῥᾳδίως ἐστίν [Oude gar neottia gypos entychein rhadiōs estin]. For it is not easy to come upon a vulture's nest. But Aelian is far more absurd in the History, book 2, chapter 46: Λέγουσι δὲ νεοττιὰν μὴ ὑποπλέκειν γῦπα [Legousi de neottian mē hypoplekein gypa], They say that the vulture does not weave a nest. What then? Γῦπας δὲ [Gypas de], he says a little later, ὠὰ μὴ τίκτειν πέπεισμαι [ōa mē tiktein pepeismai] (var. πέπυσμαι [pepysmai]), νεοττοὺς δὲ ὠδίνειν, καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ γενεᾶς κατάπτεροί εἰσι, καὶ τοῦτο ἤκουσα [neottous de ōdinein, kai hōs apo geneas katapteroi eisi, kai touto ēkousa]; I believe (or I have heard) that vultures do not hatch eggs, but bear young which are winged immediately after birth. And Philes, chapter 2:

Στρουθοὺς πτερωτοὺς ἄρ᾽ ἀπὸ μήτρας ἐξάγει, Οἱ ζῶσιν εὐθὺς ἐξ ὀνύχων ἁρπάγων, Πνίγους καλιῶν εὑρεθέντες κρείττονες. [Strouthous pterōtous ar᾽ apo mētras exagei, Hoi zōsin euthys ex onychōn harpagōn, Pnigous kaliōn heurethentes kreittones.]

It brings forth winged young from the womb, who at once procure their food with rapacious talons, being found superior to the stifling of the nest. But everyone sees whence these monstrous opinions arose. Because vultures' nests are rarely seen, some believed that they exist only in another world, others that they exist nowhere.

What Damir says of the rachama also fits the vulture, namely that it lays either a single egg or at most two. For Aristotle says of the vulture in History, book 6, chapter 5, Τίκτουσι δὲ δύο ὠὰ οἱ γῦπες [Tiktousi de dyo ōa hoi gypes], Vultures lay two eggs. And in book 9, chapter 11, Τίκτει δ᾽ ἓν ὠὸν, ἢ δύο τὰ πλεῖστα· [Tiktei d' hen ōon, ē dyo ta pleista] It lays one egg, or at most two. Pliny, in the place cited above: Their young are indeed often seen, usually in pairs.

It is also characteristic of the vulture, as we read of the rachama in the Bellunensis, that it eats putrid flesh; and in Alkazuinius, تطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من [taṭīru khalfa al-ʿasākir li-taʾkula min] [III, 62] جيف [jiyaf] It flies behind armies in order to feed on corpses. Hence in Homer, throughout, those who have been slain
— — γῦπες ἔδονται [gypes edontai],
the vultures devour. And the same men are said to be
— — γύπεσσιν πολὺ φίλτεροι, ἢ ἀλόχοισιν [gypessin poly philteroi, ē alochoisin],

far dearer to the vultures than to their wives. Indeed, on the testimony of Herodorus of Pontus in Plutarch, Roman Questions, Question 93, the vulture οὐδενὸς ἅπτεται ζῶντος, χρῆται δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀποθανοῦσιν [oudenos haptetai zōntos, chrētai de tois allois apothanousin], touches nothing living, but feeds only on the dead. Hence Lucretius, book 4, line 680:
Though bees are drawn from far by the scent of honey, And vultures by corpses. — —
Ovid, Tristia, book 1, Elegy 5:
Or as the greedy vulture looks about for some body That it can see lying beneath no earth.
Silius, book 13, line 396:
Here are the dread birds, and the vulture fed on corpses.
Gregory of Nazianzus, Poem 163, On the Adornment of Women:
— — νεκροῖς ἀμφιέπουσι γῦπες [nekrois amphiepousi gypes], — — the vulture, of course, loves a corpse.
Prudentius, Περὶ στεφάνων [Peri stephanōn], Hymn 9:
And the bite of vultures, far more effective [col. 309] At devouring morsels of dead flesh.

Plutarch, On Natural Causes, Question 26: Τὰ κενέβρια τὸν γῦπα κινεῖ, καὶ προσάγεται πόῤῥωθεν· [Ta kenebria ton gypa kinei, kai prosagetai porrhōthen] Carrion flesh stirs the vulture and draws it from afar. And in the book On Profiting from One's Enemies: Καθάπερ οἱ γῦπες ἐπὶ τὰς ὀσμὰς τῶν διεφθορότων σωμάτων φέρονται· [Kathaper hoi gypes epi tas osmas tōn diephthorotōn sōmatōn pherontai] As vultures are borne towards the smell of corpses. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 46: Γὺψ νεκρῷ πολέμιος, ἐσθίει γοῦν ἐμπεσὼν, ὡς ἐχθρόν· [Gyps nekrō polemios, esthiei goun empesōn, hōs echthron] The vulture is hostile to the dead, and falling upon it devours it as if it were an enemy. It is moreover believed to foresee those who will soon die. Aelian in the same place: Φυλάσσει τεθνηξόμενον. καὶ μέν τοι καὶ ταῖς ἐκδήμοις στρατιαῖς ἕπονται γῦπες, καὶ μάλα μαντικῶς, ὅτι γε εἰς πόλεμον χωροῦσιν εἰδότες, καὶ ὅτι μάχη πᾶσα ἐργάζεται νεκροὺς, καὶ τοῦτο ἐγνωκότες· [Phylassei tethnēxomenon. kai men toi kai tais ekdēmois stratiais hepontai gypes, kai mala mantikōs, hoti ge eis polemon chōrousin eidotes, kai hoti machē pasa ergazetai nekrous, kai touto egnōkotes] It watches one who is about to die. Vultures also follow armies marching abroad, by a kind of foreknowledge, since they know that they are setting out for war, and know this too, that every battle produces some slaughter. Philes, On Animals, chapter 2: [III, 63] Πλὴν μαντικὴν ἔχουσιν οἱ γῦπες φύσιν· Καὶ γὰρ συνεκδημοῦσι τοῖς μαχουμένοις, Τῶν σωμάτων ἐλπίδι πεσουμένων τότε. [Plēn mantikēn echousin hoi gypes physin; kai gar synekdēmousi tois machoumenois, tōn sōmatōn elpidi pesoumenōn tote.]

Moreover, vultures have a prophetic nature: for they travel abroad with those who are about to fight, in hope of the corpses that will then fall. In Pliny, Umbricius, the most skilled of the haruspices, reports that they fly three or two days beforehand to where there will be corpses. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, in the scene Piscis:
— — see how now, like vultures, they foretell three days beforehand on what day they will eat.

The Egyptians assert that vultures mark out the place of a battle not three days but seven days beforehand, and that they even foresee on which side the greater slaughter will be. Horus, Hieroglyphics book 1, chapter 11: Πολέμου μέλλοντος τελειοῦσθαι, τὸν τόπον ὁρίζει, ἐν ᾧ μέλλει ὁ πόλεμος γίνεσθαι, πρὸ ἡμέρων ἑπτὰ ἐπ' αὐτὸν παραγινομένη· [polemou mellontos teleiousthai, ton topon horizei, en hō mellei ho polemos ginesthai, pro hēmerōn hepta ep' auton paraginomenē] When the time for waging a war is at hand, it marks out the place in which the battle is to be joined, coming to it seven days beforehand. And again: Πλείονας σφαζομένους, καὶ ἡττωμένους, βλέπει, ταμιευομένη τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐκ τῶν πτωμάτων τροφήν· παρ' ὃ καὶ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι βασιλεῖς κατασκόπους ἔπεμπον σκεπτομένους κατὰ ποῖον τοῦ πολέμου οἱ γῦπες βλέπουσι μέρος, ἐντεῦθεν σημειούμενοι τοὺς ἡττωμένους. [pleionas sphazomenous, kai hēttōmenous, blepei, tamieuomenē tēn heautou ek tōn ptōmatōn trophēn; par' ho kai hoi archaioi basileis kataskopous epempon skeptomenous kata poion tou polemou hoi gypes blepousi meros, enteuthen sēmeioumenoi tous hēttōmenous] It foresees where more are to be slain, and who are to be defeated, so as to set aside food for itself from the corpses. Accordingly the ancient kings used to send out scouts to observe towards which part of the battle line the vultures were looking, and to infer from this who were to be defeated. These things, as being at least partly true, are greatly marvelled at by those Fathers who wrote on the Hexaemeron. Basil, Homily 8: Τίς τοῖς γυψὶ προαπαγγέλλων τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν θάνατον, ὅταν κατ' ἀλλήλων ἐπιστρατεύσωσιν; ἴδοις γὰρ ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὅπλων παρασκευῆς τεκμαιρομένων τὴν ἔκβασιν. [tis tois gypsi proapangellōn tōn anthrōpōn ton thanaton, hotan kat' allēlōn epistrateusōsin? idois gar an myrias agelas gypōn tois stratopedois parepomenas, ek tēs tōn hoplōn paraskeuēs tekmairomenōn tēn ekbasin] Ambrose rendered this as follows: I will ask you, and you answer me: How is it that vultures are accustomed to announce the death of men by certain signs? By what indication have they been taught and instructed that, when opposing armies begin a lamentable war against each other, these birds follow in a great flock, having foretold it, and thereby signify that a multitude of men will fall in the war, to become prey for the vultures? And Eustathius: Ἡνίκα δέ φασιν ἄνδρες εἰς πόλεμον παρατάσσονται, ἐπακολουθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καὶ οὐκ ἀφίσταται, σαρκοβόρος ὤν· [hēnika de phasin andres eis polemon paratassontai, epakolouthei autois, kai ouk aphistatai, sarkoboros ōn] But when men are drawn up in battle array, it follows and does not depart, since it is greedy for flesh. Hence legacy hunters are compared to vultures. In this sense Seneca says in Epistle 95: He is a vulture, he is waiting for a corpse. And Martial, book 6, Epigram 62:

Whose vulture will this carcass be? [col. 310] [III, 64] I add one thing: instead of רחם racham, in Deuteronomy we read רחמה rachama, with a feminine ending. For I do not agree with those who hold that the He in רחמה is paragogic, since I know that in Arabic too the feminine رخمة [rakhama] rachama occurs far more often than the masculine رخم [rakham] racham. And, as Damir notes, الها فيها للجنس [al-hā fīhā li-l-jins] in that word the letter He pertains to the genus, lest it be thought to be the He of unity, as commonly among the Arabs. But, what is more surprising, although in Greek one says ὁ γὺψ [ho gyps] in the masculine gender, yet in the Greek version of Horapollo, an Egyptian writer, ἡ γύψ [hē gyps] is always read, evidently so that the Greek word should correspond to the Egyptian רחמה rachama, or to another word analogous to it, which was feminine. This seems to have arisen from a popular error, since most Egyptians were persuaded that all vultures are female, and that they conceive in no other way than by facing the south wind, or the east wind, when it blows. Horus, Hieroglyphica, book 1, chapter 11: Ἄῤῥεν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ ὑπάρχει [Arrhen en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei], In this kind of animal there is no male. And after relating that other birds conceive from the wind eggs fit only for eating, not also for generation, he says: Γυπῶν δὲ οὐχ' ὑπηνέμιον ποιουμένων τὴν ὀχείαν ἡ τῶν ὠῶν γένεσις ζωογονεῖται [Gypōn de ouch hypēnemion poioumenōn tēn ocheian hē tōn ōōn genesis zōogoneitai], But in vultures, although they make a wind-borne union (that is, although they conceive in no other way than from the wind: for instead of οὐχ [ouch] I read κἂν [kan], or εἰ καὶ [ei kai], or something of the kind), a living creature is nevertheless generated from their eggs. Plutarch in the Roman Questions, Question 93: Εἰ δὲ (ὡς Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογοῦσι) θῆλυ πᾶν τὸ γένος ἐστὶ καὶ κυΐσκονται δεχόμενοι καταπνέοντα τὸν Ἀπηλιώτην· [Ei de (hōs Aigyptioi mythologousi) thēly pan to genos esti kai kyiskontai dechomenoi katapneonta ton Apēliōtēn] If it is true, as the Egyptians relate, that the whole race of vultures is female, and that they conceive by receiving the blast of the east wind. Ammianus, book 17, on the Egyptians: By the vulture they express the word for nature, because natural science records that no males can be found among these birds. Perhaps instead of naturae [nature] we should read matris [mother], as in Homer: Μητέρα δὲ γράφοντες γῦπα ζωγραφοῦσι, ἐπειδὴ ἄῤῥην ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ' ὑπάρχει [Mētera de graphontes gypa zōgraphousi, epeidē arrhēn en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei]. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 12, History 439, after relating this very thing much more fully, declares that he drew it ἐξ Αἰγυπτίων [ex Aigyptiōn], from the Egyptians. This fable, then, first arose in Egypt; from there it gradually spread to the other nations, especially after the birth of Christ, since many doctors of the church eagerly embraced it, or at least used it as an argumentum ad hominem, as they call it, against those who denied that Christ could have been born of a virgin. Accordingly, that female vultures conceive and bear without intercourse is written, from the choir of the Fathers, by Tertullian against the Valentinians, chapter 10; Origen against Celsus, book 1; Basil on the Hexaemeron, book 5, chapter 20; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, page 27; Procopius on Isaiah; Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7. To these may be added Theophylact Simocatta, Physical Question 8; Philes, and Pisides in the Iambics (which others attribute to Cyril of Alexandria); Peter Damian, book 2, Letter 18; Tzetzes, as above; the Etymologicum, [III, 65] Cyril the lexicographer, the Scholiasts whom we have cited, etc. Nor do I doubt that this opinion, however false and absurd, already prevailed among many from the time of Moses. Far be it from us, however, to think that Moses, swept away by that torrent, ever imagined any such thing about the vulture, even in a dream. I mean only this: that in Deu- [col. 311] teronomy he used the feminine word רחמה rachama in order to speak with the common people. But, lest anyone should turn this into a defence of the error, in Exodus he said רחם racham in the masculine.

notes.text: A most accurate description of this bird, which the Arabs call Rachaeme, was given by Hasselquist in his Travels, p. 286–289 of the German trans.; he gave it the name Vultur percnopterus, capite nudo, gula plumulosa [with naked head, downy throat], and under this name it also appears in the System. Linn. vol. 1, part 1, p. 249.
